newsitem.title: FRANCE: French politician breaches taboo on minimum wage.
newsitem.headline: French politician breaches taboo on minimum wage.

text.p: A senior French conservative politician broke a political taboo in a sensitive election period by saying in an interview released on Tuesday he saw no point in France's minimum wage.

Rene Monory, speaker of the Senate (upper house) and a former centre-right economics minister, told the magazine Passages the minimum wage, backed by a broad left-right consensus in France, was bound to disappear.

Asked whether he believed there would one day be a European Union-wide minimum hourly pay, Monory said: "Of course not. On the contrary, there will be no minimum wage at all. In any case, I no longer believe in a minimum wage in France."
The left-wing opposition and trade unions could seize on his comments in the campaign for snap parliamentary elections on May 25 and June 1.
Right-wing economists often cite the 6,400-franc ($1,120) monthly minimum pay for a 39-hour week as a major barrier to employment in a country with a record 12.8 percent jobless rate.

But conservative governments have never dared touch the SMIC -- an acronym for Indexed Minimum Inter-Professional Wage. When prime minister Edouard Balladur tried to introduce a lower rate for young job trainees in 1994, he sparked huge street protests by young people and had to withdraw the plan.
Monory said in the interview: "I am going to shock some, but is it better to pay someone 4,500 francs a month instead of 6,000 francs or to have a million young people unemployed.
"We cannot go on multiplying the number of unemployed on the excuse of protecting acquired social rights," he said.

Monory acknowledged that there was no majority in France for such radical change, but he said: "The only viable economic solution is liberalism. I would develop flexibility by giving much, much more freedom to companies.
"I far prefer limited-term contracts to no jobs at all. I would rather see a young person hired for two years than spending two years on the dole," he said.
France's curse was that, whenever there was the slightest problem, people turned to the state, which had acquired too much power, Monory added.
